record.original_question: Is every holomorphic polynomial map P:C^2 -> C^2 with everywhere nonvanishing Jacobian necessarily biholomorphic?

evidence.quote: Problem 9.2.1 If P: C2 → C2 is a holomorphic polynomial map with nonvanishing Jacobian, then P is biholomorphic.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $P:\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}^2$ be a polynomial map, i.e. $P(z_1,z_2)=(P_1(z_1,z_2),P_2(z_1,z_2))$ where $P_1,P_2\in\mathbb{C}[z_1,z_2]$. Suppose that the Jacobian determinant
$$J_P(z_1,z_2)=\det\begin{pmatrix}\partial P_1/\partial z_1 & \partial P_1/\partial z_2\\ \partial P_2/\partial z_1 & \partial P_2/\partial z_2\end{pmatrix}$$
is a nonzero constant (equivalently, never vanishes on $\mathbb{C}^2$). Prove or disprove: $P$ is necessarily a biholomorphism of $\mathbb{C}^2$ onto itself (equivalently, $P$ admits a polynomial inverse).
artifact.status_search_result: The two-dimensional Jacobian conjecture remains a celebrated open problem. Despite many partial results and reductions (e.g., reductions to degree-bounded cases, results for low-degree maps, and Moh's bound for degrees up to 100), no proof or counterexample is known as of 2026. Numerous claimed proofs have appeared but none has been accepted by the mathematical community.

status_evidence.title: Jacobian conjecture - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The Jacobian conjecture is a famous unsolved problem... even the two variable case has resisted all attempts.
status_evidence.claim: The 2D Jacobian conjecture is widely cited as an open problem.
